title: Eleven of eighteen
hook: Would you compare replication percentages without their sample sizes?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Translate 11 of 18 into a proportion and state its limited experiment sample.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Translate 11 of 18 into a proportion and state its limited experiment sample.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: In an illustrative sample, eleven of eighteen experiments replicate. What fraction is that, approximately? Toy inputs A=[11, 18]; B=[6, 10].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[61.111111111111114, 11, 18], [60, 6, 10]]. Labels: Replicated %, Replicated n, Attempted n.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The denominator is the number attempted in this specific sample. A rounded proportion is not a universal success rate for all economics or all science. The comparison shows how a different small sample can yield a nearby percentage.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Replicated=6, Attempted=10. What is Replicated %? Answer: 60.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Replicated=6, Attempted=10. What is Replicated %?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 60. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.section: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceProvenance.text: 11 of 18 lab experiments in top economics journals replicated, about 61% (Camerer et al., 2016).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Translate 11 of 18 into a proportion and state its limited experiment sample.
